concepts.name: Grid Iron / Chessboard Street Pattern: Structure and Significance
key_dimensions: Orientation of streets — cardinal directions (north-south and east-west) and their urban planning implications
Streets dividing the city into rectangular or square blocks and what this implies about centralized urban authority
Comparison with contemporary civilizations (Mesopotamia, Egypt) — absence of similar grid planning
UPSC trap: distinguishing grid pattern as a planned feature vs. organic growth seen in other ancient cities

concepts.name: Citadel vs. Lower Town: Functional and Spatial Distinction
key_dimensions: Western elevated mound (Citadel) vs. eastern lower town — physical layout and relative sizes
Citadel as administrative/ritual centre; Lower Town as residential/commercial zone
Evidence for the distinction: presence of Great Bath, granaries on citadel vs. residential structures below
UPSC trap: not all sites follow the strict two-mound pattern — exceptions like Dholavira (three divisions) must be noted

concepts.name: Standardization of Brick Sizes Across Sites
key_dimensions: Uniform ratio of brick dimensions (1:2:4) found across geographically distant sites — Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Kalibangan
Implications for a centralized authority or shared cultural/technical norms
Use of burnt bricks vs. mud bricks — contextual variation (flood-prone areas used more burnt bricks)
UPSC trap: standardization of bricks is often confused with standardization of weights and measures — these are separate but related phenomena

concepts.name: Underground Covered Drainage System: Design and Engineering
key_dimensions: Brick-lined drains running beneath main streets covered with stone or brick slabs — first known planned sewage system
Gradient design allowing flow of wastewater — evidence of understanding hydraulic engineering
Inspection holes / manholes at regular intervals for maintenance — implies civic administration
Comparison with contemporaries: Mesopotamian cities lacked comparable covered drainage systems

concepts.name: Household Drainage Connectivity to Main Drains
key_dimensions: Individual house drains connecting to street drains through soakpits or direct outlets in the lower part of walls
Implication of municipal regulation — houses could not discharge waste directly onto streets
Evidence of public health consciousness as a civic norm
UPSC trap: private wells and bathing platforms in houses are sometimes confused with public drainage — distinct features

concepts.name: The Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro: Structure and Interpretations
key_dimensions: Precise dimensions (approximately 12m x 7m x 2.4m), construction materials — burnt bricks, gypsum mortar, bitumen lining for waterproofing
Location on the citadel — implies ritual/religious rather than purely utilitarian function
Theories: ritual purification, priestly bathing, connection to later Vedic/Hindu concepts of sacred bathing
UPSC trap: Great Bath is at Mohenjo-daro only — no identical structure at Harappa; Dholavira has a large water reservoir but different in nature

concepts.name: Granaries: Location, Design, and Administrative Implications
key_dimensions: Granaries at Mohenjo-daro (on citadel), Harappa (near river, with working floors), and Lothal (near the dockyard)
Raised platforms, air ducts beneath — evidence of sophisticated storage technology
Interpreted as state-controlled surplus storage — implying redistributive economy or taxation in kind
UPSC trap: some scholars dispute the 'granary' identification at Mohenjo-daro; recent interpretations suggest it may have been a large hall

concepts.name: Water Supply: Wells and Their Urban Distribution
key_dimensions: Large number of private and public wells — Mohenjo-daro had over 700 wells, unusually high for any ancient city
Cylindrical brick-lined wells with consistent construction technique across sites
Implication of high population density and organized water management
Distinction between public wells (in open spaces/streets) and private wells (within households)

concepts.name: Dholavira's Unique Town Planning: Three-Division Layout
key_dimensions: Dholavira divided into three parts — Citadel, Middle Town, Lower Town — unlike the typical two-division pattern
Massive stone walls and gateways — use of stone rather than brick (adaptation to local geology)
Elaborate water conservation system — series of reservoirs cut into rock, unique to Dholavira
UPSC trap: Dholavira is in Gujarat (Rann of Kutch), often confused with Lothal which is also in Gujarat but a port city

concepts.name: Lothal's Dockyard: Design, Location, and Debates
key_dimensions: Rectangular basin (218m x 37m) with inlet and outlet channels — interpreted as the world's earliest known dockyard
Location near the river Bhogava — connected to Gulf of Khambhat for maritime trade
SR Rao's identification as a dockyard vs. critics who suggest it was a large irrigation tank or flood reservoir
UPSC trap: Lothal is a port site — its town planning differs from inland sites; also has a warehouse on the acropolis

concepts.name: Absence of Monumental Temples or Palaces: Governance Implications
key_dimensions: Unlike Mesopotamia and Egypt, no confirmed temple complexes or royal palace structures identified
Implies either a theocratic system without monumental expression OR a civic/merchant oligarchy rather than divine kingship
The Great Bath and Assembly Hall are the closest to public monumental structures
UPSC trap: absence of evidence is not evidence of absence — this remains a live debate in scholarship; UPSC tests understanding of the debate, not a fixed conclusion

concepts.name: Standardized Weights and Measures: Urban Trade Regulation
key_dimensions: Cubical stone weights following a binary system (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32...) in lower denominations and decimal in higher
Uniformity across sites from Baluchistan to Gujarat — implies inter-city commercial regulation
Use of a standardized unit of length (Indus inch ~3.35 cm) evidenced by ivory scales at Lothal and Mohenjo-daro
UPSC trap: standardized weights ≠ evidence of a single political empire; it may reflect shared mercantile culture

concepts.name: Orientation and Planning Authority: Evidence of Centralized Urban Governance
key_dimensions: Consistent grid orientation, uniform bricks, standard weights across 2,500+ km range suggests supralocal authority
Absence of warfare imagery, weapons, or fortification walls in lower towns — implies a relatively peaceful, regulated urban order
Debate: priest-king figurine from Mohenjo-daro as possible evidence of theocratic urban administration
UPSC trap: IVC had defensive walls around the citadel — but these are not military fortifications in the conventional sense

concepts.name: Public and Private Space Demarcation in IVC Cities
key_dimensions: Narrow lanes vs. wide main streets — hierarchy of road widths implying planned zoning
Houses opening onto side lanes, not main streets — privacy norm embedded in town planning
Presence of assembly halls and public baths vs. private bathing platforms — distinction between public and private amenity
Implications for social organization: nuclear family units in individual houses vs. communal facilities

concepts.name: House Architecture: Layout, Materials, and Social Inference
key_dimensions: Courtyard-centred house design with rooms arranged around a central open space — resemblance to later South Asian architectural tradition
Two-storey structures evidenced by staircases and thick walls at Mohenjo-daro
Uniform use of burnt bricks with evidence of plastered walls and wooden superstructures
UPSC trap: houses had no windows opening to the main street — only small ventilation openings — contrast with Mesopotamian city houses

concepts.name: Sewage and Waste Disposal: Soakpits and Rubbish Jars
key_dimensions: Soakpits lined with pottery sherds or perforated jars for liquid waste disposal at house level
Rubbish bins / collection jars at street corners — evidence of organized solid waste disposal
Stratified deposits showing repeated resurfacing of streets — evidence of urban maintenance
UPSC trap: the drainage system handled wastewater, not necessarily sewage in the modern sense — scholars debate whether toilets were connected to drains

concepts.name: Kalibangan's Unique Town Planning Features
key_dimensions: Pre-Harappan ploughed field discovered at Kalibangan — oldest known ploughed field in the world
Citadel had both a ritual area (fire altars) and a residential section — dual-functional citadel unique among IVC sites
Lower town had grid streets and a drainage system but mud brick construction instead of burnt brick
UPSC trap: Kalibangan is in Rajasthan on the banks of the Ghaggar (ancient Saraswati?) — its location is frequently asked

concepts.name: Decline of Urban Planning Standards in Later IVC Phases
key_dimensions: Evidence from upper strata at Mohenjo-daro shows degraded urban planning — huts built over streets, drains blocked, overcrowding
Interpreted as urban decay linked to IVC decline — whether caused by floods, climate change, Aryan invasion (now largely discredited), or internal collapse
Contrast between the mature Harappan phase (peak urban planning) and the late Harappan phase (de-urbanization)
UPSC trap: the Aryan invasion theory as a cause of IVC decline is now largely rejected by mainstream archaeology — Wheeler's 'massacre victims' at Mohenjo-daro reinterpreted

concepts.name: Fire Altars at Kalibangan and Lothal: Religious Dimensions of Town Planning
key_dimensions: Rows of fire altars found on the citadel at Kalibangan — suggesting organized ritual activity integrated into urban layout
Fire altar at Lothal within a house — private vs. public ritual space distinction
Debate on whether these indicate proto-Vedic fire worship or a distinct IVC ritual tradition
UPSC trap: fire altars are specific to certain sites — do not generalize as a pan-IVC feature

concepts.name: Rakhigarhi: Emerging Significance in IVC Town Planning Studies
key_dimensions: Rakhigarhi in Haryana — possibly the largest IVC site by area, larger than Mohenjo-daro and Harappa
Recent excavations (post-2015) revealing elaborate drainage, grid streets, and cemetery data
Ancient DNA studies from Rakhigarhi cemetery challenging Aryan migration theories — significant for UPSC current affairs-history overlap
UPSC trap: Rakhigarhi's size claim is recent and may not yet be fully settled — note it as 'possibly largest' rather than confirmed
